facts.claim: "notice me (feat. BENEE)" is track 4 on ROLE MODEL's six-track EP "oh, how perfect", released November 13, 2019, with a runtime of 3:12 and a copyright line of Interscope Records.
AllMusic lists the songwriting credits for "Notice Me" as Stella Rose Bennett (BENEE's real name), Happy Perez and Tucker Pillsbury.
The song was produced by Benjamin (Benji) Miller and Happy Perez.
BENEE sings a contrasting second verse and joins ROLE MODEL on the remaining choruses.
New Zealand artist BENEE both featured on and co-wrote "notice me".
Asked in an interview how the collaboration came about, ROLE MODEL said he was a fan of BENEE. He said he had her EP track "Glitter" on repeat in his car and found her sound inspiring.
The EP's sound was filled out with live horns and string sections across its six songs, and "notice me" is its only guest feature.
In February 2020 ROLE MODEL released an acoustic version of "Notice Me". The video shows him performing it with a guitar in an empty school auditorium.
"oh, how perfect" was ROLE MODEL's second EP, after the self-released debut EP "Arizona in the Summer" (2017). It was followed by "Our Little Angel" (2020) and the debut album "Rx" (2022).
ROLE MODEL is Tucker Pillsbury, born May 15, 1997 in Cape Elizabeth, Maine, and based in Los Angeles. He was signed to Interscope Records in 2018.

research.lineage: The song sits in the confessional, strummy indie-pop and bedroom-pop scene of Gen Z singer-songwriters, which one critic compared to the teen angst of Booksmart and Euphoria.

draft:
The most honest word in **notice me** is "damn." It sits at the head of the chorus's last line, a small exhale before "Damn, can't believe you notice me," and it gives away more than any verse does. Everything around it is built to sound cool. That one word is the sound of someone who still can't believe their luck.

The first verse runs on bravado. Hands in jeans, talking dirty, making a scene on a dance floor and refusing to stop until someone throws them out. Backing voices repeat the last word of each line like friends egging the narrator on. Then the chorus arrives and the swagger turns into astonishment. The song keeps both feelings in the same body. There's the kid who wants the whole room to watch, and the kid who has spent years assuming nobody would ever look. Neither one cancels the other, and that's why the chorus feels sweet rather than smug.

The track itself stays light on its feet. A drum machine keeps a steady, driving beat with a snare that snaps up front. A bass guitar loops a simple line, a synth pad holds the chords underneath, and a clean electric guitar picks out arpeggios over the top. The tempo leans quick, with a slight swing that keeps it from marching. ROLE MODEL, the project of Tucker Pillsbury, sings in a clear, slightly nasal voice with a rhythmic, almost conversational cadence, closer to talking someone into something than belting at them. The mix is dry and polished, each part distinct, and the voices sit close.

BENEE, who co-wrote the song with Pillsbury and Happy Perez, takes the contrasting second verse. Her voice is breathy and higher, and her phrasing stretches out where his stays clipped. Her verse moves the story indoors: "Only thought I'd have you in my dreams." It's the same disbelief seen from the other side, softer and more private, ending with brown eyes and a whisper. Pillsbury has said he had her track "Glitter" on repeat in his car, and you can hear why he wanted her. She makes the crush mutual. She's the only guest on the EP *oh, how perfect*, and the song is better for having two people stunned by each other.

Then comes the confession that explains the whole thing: "Always had bad luck, never got this far." This is Gen Z bedroom pop, the confessional scene one critic tied to the teen angst of *Booksmart* and *Euphoria*. This song bends that mood toward the grin instead of the gloom. Pillsbury later filmed an acoustic take alone with a guitar in an empty school auditorium, and that room fits. It's where you go to dance when you're not supposed to.

The song captures the rush of being chosen by someone you only expected to want from a distance, and that "damn" lets you feel the swagger and the disbelief in the same breath.
